newsitem.title: FRANCE: Airbus consortium partners agree on restructuring.
newsitem.headline: Airbus consortium partners agree on restructuring.

text.p: Partners in the Airbus consortium reached a preliminary accord Friday to restructure the European plane maker to help it challenge Boeing Co., which will become an even more formidable competitor with its acquisition of McDonnell Douglas Corp.

The brief announcement of the agreement, however, did not reveal the shape the new Airbus would take and did not address disagreements among the four main partners -- British, French, German and Spanish aerospace companies.

"The partners of Airbus Industrie met today in Paris and, as a result of the progress made, a memorandum of understanding has been agreed. The MOU will be signed over the next few days," Airbus said in a statement after the meeting.
An Airbus spokeswoman refused to comment further.
Airbus is currently a Groupement d'Interet Economique, a French legal entity that makes no profits in its own right. Instead, these go to the four partners who make decisions by consensus.
The four partners are French state-owned Ste Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG, and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA.
Aerospatiale and Daimler-Benz, also known as DASA, each have a 38 percent stake in the consortium. British Aerospace has 20 percent and Construcciones Aeronauticas, known as CASA, has 4 percent.
The partners agreed last July to turn the consortium into a corporation to streamline decision-making and production.
The restructuring plans took on a more urgent tone after Boeing and McDonnell Douglas said last month they would merge and form a civil and military behemoth with nearly $50 billion in annual sales.
That deal prodded the Airbus partners to move to keep up with the rapid and far-reaching restructuring under way in the defence industry in the United States.
The partners said in July that they intended to reach an agreement by the end of 1996 on a timetable for setting up a new company that could be formed by 1999.
But the partners were deeply divided over how to structure a new company, senior industry executives have said.
Aerospatiale wants a "minimal" Airbus that would act as prime contractor with enlarged powers to direct subcontractors.
But DASA seeks to deepen Airbus integration to include design and engineering of sub-assemblies as well as making major systems such as wings and fuselages.
This "maximum Airbus" would also handle procurement, final assembly and product support.

British Aerospace wants to transfer core assets, including design and manufacturing facilities, from the partners to a new company and provide it with a strong balance sheet to finance aircraft sales, executives have said.
Another crucial issue, which Airbus made no reference to in Friday's statement, is the prospect of building a large aircraft to compete with Boeing's 747 jumbo jet.
The 747 is the only commercial jet capable of carrying more than 400 passengers and Airbus would dearly like to challenge Boeing's lone grip on a profitable segment of the market.
